citation: herdr src/config/model.rs at the v0.8.0 tag: TerminalConfig (default_shell, shell_mode), AdvancedConfig (scrollback_limit_bytes, default 10000000), UpdateConfig (version_check and manifest_check, both defaulting to true). The file is read through config_path(), which HERDR_CONFIG_PATH names - verified against the pinned binary rather than only its source.
why:
Muster's daemon used to read the user's own herdr config, so a `default_shell` set for somebody's terminal decided what every Muster pane ran, scrollback depth was unreachable from Muster's file, and the daemon Muster pinned by checksum took its update policy from a file Muster does not own. It now reads a file Muster writes.

That makes this the backend's half of an arrangement the renderer already has: no dependency here takes a value except as a file, so Muster derives one and names it. These cases are the translation - Muster's two settings on the left, the daemon's words on the right - and they are the only place the mapping is pinned, because herdr exposes no way to read its config back. What a real daemon proves instead is the consequence: a pane runs the shell Muster named. That test lives beside this file; these cases are what it is a consequence of.

Two policies are pinned here rather than left to be rediscovered. `version_check` is written off unconditionally and is not a setting anybody may change, so a file with nothing configured is still a file. And a default herdr already holds is never restated - `shell_mode = auto`, `new_cwd = follow` - because Muster restating a default it agrees with is how a daemon's changed mind becomes invisible.

**`manifest_check` is the third policy, and it is the one that is absent.** Muster wrote it off for a year on the reasoning that pins its binary, and the two are not the same subject. A manifest is data describing how a third-party agent looks on screen, and those agents change on their own schedule: Claude Code moved its busy spinner from Braille to a half-circle, the only rule in herdr's bundled claude manifest that can produce `working` matches Braille in the terminal title, and `working` became unreachable on every machine. Eleven agent transitions across a full day of real use on two machines, and `working` was not among them - in a product whose founding desideratum is that the dot says what an agent is doing. Upstream had published a corrected manifest two days earlier and this file was what stopped it arriving (kan a_2HxSqYtuA). Nothing here says `manifest_check`, so herdr's own default stands and a daemon tracks the rules for the agents somebody is actually running. The suite is unaffected: `herdr-harness` and the probe write their own config with both checks off, so a recorded corpus is still judged against frozen rules.

cases.name: a person who configured nothing still gets a daemon pinned to its version
cases.why:
The case that says why this file exists at all, and the one difference from the renderer's derived config, which is skipped entirely when there is nothing to say. `version_check` defaults to true in herdr, so a daemon Muster downloaded, verified against a checksum and staged inside its own bundle would go looking for a different version of itself. Pinning it is the whole reason a green suite is a statement about anything, and an update check is the one thing that moves it off the pin without anybody asking.

`manifest_check` is absent, and the absence is what this case pins: it defaults to true in herdr too, and Muster used to write it off beside `version_check` as though they were one subject. They are not. A version is the binary the corpus was recorded against; a manifest is data describing how a third-party agent looks on screen. Freezing the second bought nothing and cost `working` - see the file's `why` for the measurement.

cases.name: what a pane runs, said once in Muster's file
cases.why: The motivating case for the second of the three complaints. Somebody with `default_shell` set for their own terminal was silently deciding what every Muster pane ran, and the corpus was recorded against neither that answer nor any other. Now the daemon is told, and the file that tells it is one Muster wrote.

cases.name: a mode the daemon already defaults to is not restated
cases.why: `auto` is herdr's own answer, so writing it down would be Muster pinning a default it has no opinion about - and the day herdr changes that default is the day Muster should notice rather than silently keep the old one. The same reasoning `pane.zoom` uses for leaving `mode` off the wire.

cases.name: how deep a pane's history goes, in the bytes the buffer is measured in
cases.why: The motivating case for the first complaint: wanting deeper scrollback meant learning herdr existed and finding its config file. herdr's key is `scrollback_limit_bytes` and Muster's is `scrollback_bytes`, which is a rename rather than a conversion - both are bytes, so the number a person writes is the number the buffer gets.

cases.name: a pane that remembers nothing is written down rather than left out
cases.why: Zero and absent mean different things here and would be indistinguishable if the writer treated a falsy value as unset: absent is herdr's ten megabytes, and zero is a pane that keeps only what is on screen. Somebody who does not want an agent's output sitting in a buffer asked for the second one.

cases.why: The whole vocabulary at once, which is what makes the block ordering a decision rather than an accident: `[terminal]` before `[advanced]` before `[update]`, so that a file read top to bottom goes from what a pane is, to how much of it is kept, to the one thing nobody may change.

cases.name: a shell path with a quote in it survives into the daemon's file
cases.why: A path can hold a quote or a backslash, and a writer that pasted the string in raw would produce a file herdr cannot parse - which fails silently, because herdr keeps its defaults and reports a diagnostic to a log nobody is reading. Escaped by hand rather than with Rust's own debug spelling, whose `\u{1b}` is not something TOML reads.
